chapter_title: Setting Up Your VR Development Environment
chapter_summary:
Embarking on your VR development journey with Unity requires a properly configured environment, which forms the bedrock of all your immersive creations. Before writing a single line of code or placing a single 3D model, you need to ensure Unity is ready to communicate with your chosen VR headset. This typically involves several steps, starting with the Unity Editor itself. You should have a recent LTS (Long Term Support) version of Unity installed, as these versions offer the most stability and up-to-date XR features. Once Unity is installed, the next critical step is configuring the XR Plugin Management system, which is Unity's modern approach to handling various VR SDKs (Software Development Kits) like Oculus, OpenXR, or Windows Mixed Reality.

To begin, open your Unity project (or create a new 3D project) and navigate to `Edit > Project Settings`. In the Project Settings window, select `XR Plug-in Management`. Here, you'll see a list of available plug-in providers. For most modern VR development, especially targeting devices like the Meta Quest, you'll want to enable `Oculus` and/or `OpenXR`. OpenXR is an open standard that aims to unify VR/AR development across different platforms, offering a more future-proof approach. When you enable a plug-in provider, Unity might prompt you to install necessary packages, which you should accept. For instance, enabling Oculus will install the `Meta XR SDK` (formerly Oculus XR Plugin), and enabling OpenXR will install the `OpenXR Plugin`. It's crucial to select the correct plug-in for your target hardware. If you're developing for a Meta Quest headset, enabling the Oculus plug-in is paramount. If you're aiming for broader compatibility or SteamVR, OpenXR is a strong choice.

After configuring the XR Plug-in Management, the next indispensable component is the XR Interaction Toolkit. This toolkit provides a high-level, component-based system for common VR interactions such as grabbing, teleporting, and UI interaction, significantly simplifying the development process. To install it, go to `Window > Package Manager`. Ensure the dropdown in the top-left is set to "Unity Registry." Search for "XR Interaction Toolkit" and install the latest verified version. Once installed, you might be prompted to import starter assets, which include useful prefabs and input action maps; it's generally a good idea to import these. The toolkit relies on Unity's Input System, so you might also need to install the `Input System` package if it's not already present. Upon installing the Input System, Unity will ask if you want to switch to the new input system; confirm this, and Unity will restart.

With the XR Interaction Toolkit in place, you can now set up your basic VR scene. The central component for any VR experience in Unity using the XR Interaction Toolkit is the `XR Origin`. This prefab acts as the player's head and hands in the virtual world. You can add it to your scene by right-clicking in the Hierarchy window, selecting `XR > XR Origin (VR/Desktop)`. This prefab comes pre-configured with a Camera Offset (which represents the user's head), and two XR Controllers (one for each hand), along with the necessary locomotion and input components. The XR Origin handles the tracking of the headset and controllers, ensuring your virtual camera matches the user's head movements and your virtual hands respond to controller input. You'll notice that the XR Origin has an `XR Origin` component, an `Input Action Manager`, and often `Locomotion System` components. The `Input Action Manager` is responsible for processing input from your physical controllers and mapping them to defined actions, such as "Grab" or "Teleport."

A common mistake beginners make is neglecting to correctly set up the `Input Action Manager` or forgetting to enable the appropriate input actions. The XR Interaction Toolkit provides default Input Action Assets (e.g., `XRI Default Input Actions`), which define actions like "Move," "Turn," "Select," and "Grab." These assets need to be assigned to the `Input Action Manager` component on your XR Origin, and the actions within them must be enabled. If your controllers aren't responding, always check the `Input Action Manager` and the `XR Controller` components to ensure they are correctly configured and referencing the right input actions. Another frequent issue is scale. VR experiences often require careful attention to scale to prevent discomfort. Ensure your environment and models are built to a realistic scale relative to the `XR Origin` (which typically represents a human-sized player). If your virtual world feels too big or too small, it can quickly lead to motion sickness. Always test your scale early and often. Finally, remember to add a `Floor` or `Ground` object to your scene. Without a visual reference for the ground, users can feel disoriented. A simple 3D Plane or Cube scaled up will suffice for initial testing.

screens.title: Setting Up Your VR Development Environment
screens.subtitle: Make Unity ready for VR: plugins, interaction toolkit, XR Origin, and practical checks

narration.text: Starting a VR project in Unity begins before any code or models. In this lesson you will learn the exact environment pieces that must be in place so your headset and Unity talk to each other reliably. We cover choosing a stable Unity LTS version, enabling the XR Plug-in Management providers you need, installing the XR Interaction Toolkit and the Input System, and adding an XR Origin so your headset and controllers are tracked. You will also learn common setup mistakes to avoid, such as missing input action assets or forgetting to delete the default camera. By the end you will be able to create a simple scene with a ground plane and an interactable cube and test it on a Meta Quest using Link. A concrete example we use throughout is adding an XR Origin prefab and assigning the XRI Default Input Actions asset so grab and teleport actions work. A frequent misconception I see is thinking the XR Origin alone makes controllers work; in practice you must also assign and enable input actions. As you explore the topic, ask yourself: can I start play mode and see head tracking and use a grip to grab the cube? If not, the checklist on later screens will guide your next steps.

keyIdea.title: Why setup matters
keyIdea.text: A correct environment ensures your headset, input mappings, and XR prefabs work together so early testing is reliable and iterative work is productive.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Setting Up Your VR Development Environment
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Setting Up Your VR Development Environment

Prepare Unity so your headset, controllers, and interaction toolkit work together. This lesson gives a practical checklist and hands-on steps to get a simple scene running.

What you will understand

Which Unity packages and prefabs to install, how to assign input actions, and how to validate tracking and grabbing with a basic cube.

Why it matters

A stable setup reduces time wasted on configuration issues and prevents false assumptions about controller or headset failures during development.

Explore Key Topics
Three topics you'll use right away to build your first test scene.
XR Plug-in Mgmt
Enable Oculus or OpenXR so Unity can load the right runtime for your headset.
XR Interaction Toolkit
Install the toolkit and starter assets for grab, teleport and input wiring.
XR Origin & Input
Add an XR Origin prefab and assign the XRI Default Input Actions to get controllers responding.
Setup Map
Checklist preview
Editor
Unity LTS
Plugins
Oculus / OpenXR
Interaction
XR Toolkit + Input
Quick tip
If controllers do not respond in Play mode, first check the Input Action Manager assignments on the XR Origin. This single check resolves many initial problems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: In this pair of objective screens you will find clear, verifiable goals tied to setup tasks you can perform. Each objective is actionable: recognize the editor and plugin choices, install required packages, add prefabs and input assets, and diagnose common startup issues. For example, you should be able to open Project Settings, enable an XR provider, accept package installs, and confirm the XR Interaction Toolkit and Input System are present. You will also practice adding an XR Origin and assigning the XRI Default Input Actions so controller actions like grab and select are bound. A common misconception is thinking install alone is enough; here you will learn the final wiring steps—assigning action assets and enabling actions—so input actually flows from the headset to your scene. These objectives prepare you to build a basic test scene and to iterate confidently when tracking or input fails. As you work through the objectives, verify each milestone by running Play mode and checking head and hand tracking, then attempting a grab interaction with the sample cube.

keyIdea.title: Verified milestones
keyIdea.text: By the end you should be able to install plugins, add XR Origin, assign input assets, and successfully test head and controller tracking in Play mode.

screens.title: Unity Editor and LTS: a stable foundation
screens.subtitle: Why a recent Unity LTS matters for VR development

narration.text: A stable editor is the foundation of a reliable VR workflow. Unity LTS versions receive stability updates and frequently include the latest XR support and verified package compatibility. In practice, choosing a recent LTS reduces the chance you will run into package conflicts when enabling XR Plug-in Management or installing the XR Interaction Toolkit. A concrete example: when a project uses an LTS editor, package prompts for installing the Meta XR SDK or OpenXR Plugin typically succeed without compatibility errors, letting you continue to the Input System and toolkit installs. A common misconception is that any Unity release will behave the same for XR; in reality, non-LTS or older editors sometimes lack verified package stability and cause restarts or package resolution failures. To check readiness, create a 3D Core project and confirm the Package Manager shows the XR Interaction Toolkit and Input System in the Unity Registry. If one is missing, you will need to change the Package Manager view to the Unity Registry and install the packages listed in the chapter. Why this matters: early stability means you can iterate on interaction design and testing instead of spending hours on configuration issues. Try this quick self-check: can you open Project Settings, find XR Plug-in Management, and see install prompts? If yes, your editor environment is ready to proceed.

keyIdea.title: Stable editor = faster iteration
keyIdea.text: Using a recent Unity LTS avoids compatibility headaches and keeps XR packages installable and stable for development.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Unity Editor and LTS
Definition

A Unity LTS is a stable release recommended for projects where package compatibility matters. For VR, LTS versions commonly host verified behavior for XR packages.

Practical check

Create a 3D project and open Package Manager. Ensure 'Unity Registry' is selected and the XR Interaction Toolkit appears available to install.

Example

If the toolkit shows as installable and prompts to import starter assets, your editor supports the workflow described in the chapter.

Misconception

Not every editor version behaves the same for XR; older or non-LTS editors can introduce package resolution problems.

Checklist
  • Start a Unity 3D Core project.
  • Open Package Manager and select Unity Registry.
  • Verify XR Interaction Toolkit and Input System are installable.
  • Confirm no package compatibility warnings appear.
Key Takeaway

Start with a recent LTS to minimize XR package conflicts so you can focus on interaction design.

screens.title: XR Plug-in Management
screens.subtitle: Enable the right runtime providers for your target headsets

narration.text: XR Plug-in Management is Unity's centralized system for integrating VR SDKs and runtimes into a project. It exposes provider lists per platform tab—Android and PC—so you enable the plug-ins suited to your target device. For example, if you are developing for a Meta Quest headset and targeting Android, you enable the Oculus provider under the Android tab. If you want broader cross-platform compatibility, enabling OpenXR is often preferable because it represents an open standard that unifies many devices under a single A P I. The practical steps are: open Edit, select Project Settings, open XR Plug-in Management, and toggle the provider(s) you need. Unity will prompt to install required packages such as the Meta XR SDK or the OpenXR Plugin; accept those prompts to add the runtime. A common mistake is enabling a provider under the wrong platform tab—double-check you're on the Android tab for Quest development. Another pitfall is ignoring the install prompts: the provider toggle adds the package to your project. The key takeaway is to select the provider that matches your hardware and to accept the package installations Unity requests, because missing runtime packages block headset communication. After installing, proceed to the next step: the XR Interaction Toolkit and input wiring.

keyIdea.title: Provider selection
keyIdea.text: Enable the plug-in provider that matches your target headset and accept Unity's package prompts to install required SDKs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › XR Plug-in Management
What it does

Offers a single place to enable VR/AR providers per build platform and to install corresponding packages Unity needs to communicate with headsets and runtimes.

Step-by-step
  1. Open Edit > Project Settings.
  2. Select XR Plug-in Management.
  3. Choose the target platform tab (Android or PC).
  4. Toggle Oculus and/or OpenXR and accept install prompts.
Common mistake

Enabling a provider under the wrong platform tab or skipping the install prompts prevents the runtime from being added to the project.

Visual checklist
OpenXR

An open standard for cross-platform compatibility; enable for broader device support.

Oculus

Enable when targeting Meta Quest devices under Android.

Key Takeaway

Match the plug-in to your target platform and install the package prompts Unity provides to enable headset communication.

screens.title: OpenXR vs Platform SDKs
screens.subtitle: Choosing between OpenXR and a vendor-specific provider

narration.text: When selecting a plug-in provider, you will often choose between an open standard provider such as OpenXR and a platform-specific SDK like the Oculus provider. OpenXR's goal is broad compatibility: by writing against OpenXR you aim to target multiple OpenXR-compliant headsets without changing core code. The chapter emphasizes OpenXR as a future-proof choice for many developers who plan to support several devices. By contrast, enabling the Oculus provider installs the Meta XR SDK which targets Meta devices such as Quest and may provide vendor-specific features. A concrete example: if your immediate target is Meta Quest and you only need Quest-specific features, enabling the Oculus provider under the Android tab and installing the Meta XR SDK is appropriate. A misconception is to assume OpenXR always replaces vendor SDKs; in some workflows you still enable vendor plugins or test vendor runtimes. The practical approach is to decide based on your target hardware: enable Oculus for Quest-focused builds, enable OpenXR for broader compatibility, and accept the package installs Unity prompts. Finally, test early: after enabling a provider, confirm Play mode tracking or a Link connection to ensure the runtime loads as expected.

keyIdea.title: Match provider to goals
keyIdea.text: OpenXR favors cross-device compatibility; vendor SDKs like Oculus can be chosen for device-specific features and direct support for that headset.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › OpenXR vs Platform SDKs
OpenXR

An open standard API aimed at cross-platform compatibility. Use it to reduce platform lock-in when supporting many headsets.

When to choose

When targeting more than one device or wanting a future-proof runtime path.

Vendor SDK (Oculus)

A provider tailored to a specific platform, such as Meta Quest. Useful when you need vendor features or tight device integration.

When to choose

When your project targets a single vendor and you need platform-specific features.

Practical tip

Decide early which provider to enable based on target hardware, then accept Unity's install prompts so the runtime packages are present for testing.

screens.title: Installing XR Interaction Toolkit & Input System
screens.subtitle: Package Manager steps and starter assets

narration.text: Installing the XR Interaction Toolkit and the Input System is a clear sequence in the Package Manager. First, open Window > Package Manager and make sure the dropdown is set to 'Unity Registry'. Search for 'XR Interaction Toolkit' and install the latest verified version. Unity often prompts to import starter assets—these include prefabs and input action maps such as the XRI Default Input Actions, which you should import to speed development. Next, search for and install the Input System package if it isn't present. When you install the Input System, Unity will prompt to switch to the new input system. Confirm this change; Unity will restart to apply the new input runtime. A concrete example: after installing both packages and accepting the restart, you should see the toolkit's prefabs appear in the package folder and an Input Action Asset in the imported starter assets. A common misconception is that the toolkit alone provides input; in fact the toolkit relies on the Input System and its action maps. If you skip the Input System installation or decline the restart, controller actions may not be processed and interactions will not function as expected. After the restart, you are ready to add an XR Origin and wire the input actions.

keyIdea.title: Install sequence
keyIdea.text: Install XR Interaction Toolkit from the Unity Registry, import starter assets, then install the Input System and accept the editor restart to enable input mappings.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Install Toolkit & Input
Steps in Package Manager
  1. Select Window > Package Manager and set view to Unity Registry.
  2. Search for 'XR Interaction Toolkit' and install the verified version.
  3. Import starter assets when prompted to get prefabs and the default action maps.
  4. Install 'Input System' if not present and accept the switch when prompted.
Example

After restart you should find XRI Default Input Actions among the imported assets and XR prefabs in the toolkit folder.

Common pitfalls
  • Skipping starter asset import loses the default action maps.
  • Declining the Input System switch prevents the toolkit from receiving controller actions.
Key Takeaway

Install toolkit, import starter assets, and switch to the Input System so actions are available to XR controllers.

screens.title: XR Origin: the player's representation
screens.subtitle: What the XR Origin prefab contains and why it matters

narration.text: The XR Origin prefab is the central player representation in scenes using the XR Interaction Toolkit. It typically contains a Camera Offset for the user's head, two XR Controllers representing left and right hands, an Input Action Manager, and locomotion or tracking components. The Camera Offset ensures that the virtual camera maps to the physical headset's position and rotation. The XR Controllers provide placeholders for selecting, grabbing, and activating objects, and each controller references specific input actions for select, activate, and grab. The Input Action Manager processes the Input Action Asset assigned to it and exposes actions like Move, Turn, Select, and Grab to other components. A concrete example from the chapter: you add an XR Origin by selecting XR > XR Origin (VR/Desktop) in the Hierarchy; then you should delete the default Main Camera because the XR Origin already includes a camera. A common mistake is leaving the Main Camera in the scene, causing duplicate cameras and unexpected behavior. Another frequent omission is not assigning the XRI Default Input Actions to the Input Action Manager, which prevents controller inputs from being recognized. The core idea is that the XR Origin is the wiring hub between physical hardware and in-scene interactions; configure it carefully to ensure tracking and input flow correctly.

keyIdea.title: XR Origin = tracking hub
keyIdea.text: XR Origin contains the camera, controllers, and Input Action Manager; assign action assets and remove the default camera to avoid conflicts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › XR Origin
Contents of XR Origin
  • Camera Offset (user head)
  • XR Controller (left and right)
  • Input Action Manager
  • Optional Locomotion System components
Action wiring

Assign an Input Action Asset to Input Action Manager so controller components receive Select, Grab, and Activate actions.

Practical steps
  1. Right-click Hierarchy and choose XR > XR Origin (VR/Desktop).
  2. Delete the default Main Camera from the scene.
  3. Select XR Origin and assign the XRI Default Input Actions to the Input Action Manager.
Gotcha

Leaving the Main Camera causes duplicate cameras; forgetting to assign input actions prevents controllers from working.

screens.title: Input Action Manager and Controller Bindings
screens.subtitle: Assign action assets and verify controller mappings

narration.text: The Input Action Manager on the XR Origin is the bridge between Unity's Input System and the XR controller components. It holds references to Input Action Assets—such as the XRI Default Input Actions—and exposes those actions to XR Controller components. If your controllers are not responding, the most likely reason is a missing or unassigned Input Action Asset. To troubleshoot, open the XR Origin, find the Input Action Manager component, and confirm an Action Asset is assigned to its Action Assets list. Next, inspect the XR Controller components under the XR Origin for left and right controllers and verify their Select Action, Activate Action, and Grab Action properties reference actions within the assigned asset. A concrete example: if a Grab is not working, check that the Grab Action exists and is enabled in the XRI Default Input Actions asset and that the XR Controller's Grab Action field is pointing to it. A common misconception is assuming the XR Controller automatically maps to controller buttons; in the new Input System you must bind physical buttons to named actions. The final check is to open the action asset and ensure the relevant actions are enabled and have bindings suitable for your headset controllers. This step-by-step wiring resolves most initial controller input problems.

keyIdea.title: Input wiring is explicit
keyIdea.text: Assign an Input Action Asset to the Input Action Manager and ensure each XR Controller references the correct action fields for grab, select, and activate.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Input Action Manager
What to verify
  • Input Action Asset assigned to Input Action Manager.
  • XR Controller select/activate/grab fields point to actions in that asset.
  • Actions in the asset are enabled and have suitable bindings for your controllers.
Example check

Open XRI Default Input Actions and confirm 'Grab' is enabled. Then inspect XR Controller's Grab Action assignment.

Troubleshooting steps
  1. Open the XR Origin and find Input Action Manager.
  2. Ensure an Input Action Asset is present in Action Assets.
  3. Open each XR Controller and confirm action references.
  4. Open the action asset and enable missing actions or adjust bindings.
Key Takeaway

Controller input requires explicit action bindings; check assignments before assuming hardware failure.

screens.title: Hands-on: create a test scene
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step to add XR Origin, ground, and an interactable cube

narration.text: Let's walk through creating a minimal test scene that verifies head tracking and grabbing. First, create a new Unity 3D project. In Project Settings open XR Plug-in Management and enable the appropriate provider for your hardware—enable Oculus under the Android tab for Meta Quest or OpenXR for broad compatibility. Next, open Window > Package Manager, ensure Unity Registry is selected, install XR Interaction Toolkit and Input System, and import the toolkit starter assets. Once the editor restarts from the Input System switch, right-click in the Hierarchy and add XR > XR Origin (VR/Desktop). Delete the default Main Camera because the XR Origin includes its own camera. Add a Plane via 3D Object > Plane, rename it Ground, set its position to (0,0,0) and scale to (10,1,10) so you have a visual floor. Add a Cube at position (0,1,2). On the Cube add a Rigidbody component and uncheck Use Gravity for initial testing, then add an XR Grab Interactable component and ensure the Collider is enabled. A common mistake is forgetting to add the Rigidbody or collider—without them the cube won't be grabbable. After these steps connect your Meta Quest with Link and press Play to verify you can look around and grab the cube. This flow gives you a reproducible quick-test environment for input and tracking.

keyIdea.title: Reproducible test scene
keyIdea.text: A simple scene with XR Origin, ground plane, and an XR Grab Interactable cube verifies tracking and input before adding complex content.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Hands-on: Test Scene
Step-by-step checklist
  1. Create new Unity 3D Core project.
  2. Enable provider in XR Plug-in Management and accept installs.
  3. Install XR Interaction Toolkit and Input System, import starter assets.
  4. Add XR Origin and delete default Main Camera.
  5. Add Plane named Ground at (0,0,0) scaled (10,1,10).
  6. Add Cube at (0,1,2) with Rigidbody (no gravity) and XR Grab Interactable.
Example scene values
Ground position 0,0,0; Ground scale 10,1,10; Cube at 0,1,2; Rigidbody with Use Gravity unchecked; XR Grab Interactable attached.
Key Takeaway

Follow these steps to create a minimal, reliable test scene that reveals tracking and input issues early.

screens.title: Physics and Interactables
screens.subtitle: Rigidbody, collider, and XR Grab Interactable essentials

narration.text: To make objects grabbable in Unity with the XR Interaction Toolkit you must provide physics components and an interactable component. The Cube example in the chapter demonstrates this: add a Rigidbody to allow physics-managed motion and keep the collider enabled so interactions detect contact. For early testing, disabling gravity prevents the cube from dropping and lets you focus on grabbing behavior. Add the XR Grab Interactable component so the toolkit can attach the object to controller motions when a grab action is triggered. A misconception is thinking the XR Grab Interactable alone is sufficient; without a Rigidbody and a collider the object cannot participate in physics or collision detection, preventing realistic grabbing. A concrete scenario: place a cube at position 0,1,2, add a Rigidbody, uncheck Use Gravity during initial tests, and add XR Grab Interactable. Verify the collider is enabled by inspecting the Cube's Collider property. If the collider is missing or disabled, the grab will fail. The core practice is to ensure colliders and Rigidbody exist before adding the XR Grab Interactable so interactions behave predictably during playtesting. Physics and Interactables means add rigidbody and collider before xr grab interactable so physics and collision detection allow grabbing to work correctly.. In practical terms, rigidbody, collider, and xr grab interactable essentials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interactable prerequisites
keyIdea.text: Add Rigidbody and Collider before XR Grab Interactable so physics and collision detection allow grabbing to work correctly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Physics & Interactables
Essentials
  • Collider must be present and enabled.
  • Rigidbody enables physics motion; uncheck Use Gravity for initial tests.
  • XR Grab Interactable attaches object to controller when Grab action triggers.
Example setup

Cube at (0,1,2) with Collider, Rigidbody, and XR Grab Interactable lets you test grabbing without objects falling away.

Common mistake

Adding only XR Grab Interactable without a Rigidbody or collider makes the object non-interactive because physics and contact detection are missing.

Key Takeaway

Always attach a collider and Rigidbody before making an object grabbable with XR components.

screens.title: Scale and floor: avoid discomfort
screens.subtitle: Set realistic scale and add a floor for spatial reference

narration.text: Scale and a clear floor reference are small details that greatly affect comfort in VR. If your environment or models are out of scale relative to the XR Origin, users can feel disoriented or experience motion sickness. The chapter recommends testing scale early by ensuring the XR Origin represents a human-sized player and that models are built with consistent real-world proportions. Add a Ground or Floor object such as a Plane or a large Cube to provide a visible reference; the sample steps suggest adding a Plane named Ground at position (0,0,0) scaled to (10,1,10). This simple plane gives users a clear visual horizon and reduces disorientation. A misconception is that scale only matters for aesthetics; in fact incorrect scale can lead to discomfort and misjudged interactions. To validate scale, put the XR Origin in the scene, press Play, and verify that the ground aligns with the user's expectation of where their feet should be. If the world feels too big or too small, rescale your models rather than modifying the XR Origin height. The practical habit is to test scale frequently, add a ground reference early, and iterate until the proportions feel natural in headset testing.

keyIdea.title: Scale affects comfort
keyIdea.text: Use a physical-scale approach and add a visible ground plane early so users have a consistent reference and avoid discomfort.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Scale & Floor
Why scale matters

Realistic scale helps users judge distances and reduces motion discomfort. Incorrect scale alters perceived speed and reach for interactions.

Practical example

Add a Plane at 0,0,0 scaled to 10,1,10 to serve as a ground reference during early tests.

Test loop
  1. Add XR Origin and ground plane.
  2. Enter Play and check perceived height and horizon in headset.
  3. Adjust model scales if the world feels oversized or miniature.
Quick Tip

Rescale models instead of shifting the XR Origin to preserve consistent tracking behavior.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common setup issues
screens.subtitle: A focused checklist for controller and tracking problems

narration.text: When Play mode doesn't show expected tracking or controller responses, follow a short, methodical checklist to identify the cause. First, confirm your XR Plug-in Management has the correct provider enabled for the platform you are testing and that Unity installed the prompted packages. Second, check the XR Origin's Input Action Manager and ensure an Input Action Asset like XRI Default Input Actions is assigned. Third, inspect the XR Controller components for left and right hands and verify that their Select, Activate, and Grab Action fields reference actions in the assigned asset. Fourth, confirm colliders and Rigidbody components are present on interactable objects; missing colliders are a common reason grabs fail. Fifth, ensure you removed the default Main Camera so the XR Origin camera is the active camera. If you are testing on Meta Quest via Link, ensure the headset link is active before pressing Play. A common misconception is blaming the headset when a missing action asset or unassigned controller field is the real cause; resolving these wiring steps usually restores input quickly. After these checks, re-run Play mode; if issues persist, revisit package installation and starter asset imports to ensure no components were skipped during setup.

keyIdea.title: Start with wiring checks
keyIdea.text: Most setup failures stem from unassigned action assets, missing colliders, or leftover default cameras; check these first.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Troubleshooting
Quick checklist
  • Confirm XR provider enabled and packages installed.
  • Check Input Action Manager has an action asset assigned.
  • Verify XR Controller action fields reference asset actions.
  • Ensure colliders and Rigidbody exist on interactables.
  • Remove default Main Camera to avoid conflicts.
Example fault

If grab does nothing, open the XRI Default Input Actions and confirm 'Grab' is present and enabled. Then confirm the XR Controller Grab Action references that action. Most fixes are resolved here.

Final Tip

Work through the wiring checklist before assuming hardware or driver problems; many issues are configuration-based.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: Meta Quest setup & test
screens.subtitle: Follow these exact steps to produce a working test on Meta Quest

narration.text: This activity bundles the chapter's steps into a single reproducible task: create a new Unity project, enable Oculus under XR Plug-in Management's Android tab, install XR Interaction Toolkit and Input System, add XR Origin and a grabbable cube, then test with Meta Quest via Link. Start by creating a new 3D Core project. Open Project Settings, navigate to XR Plug-in Management and pick the Android tab; enable Oculus and accept any install prompts. Open Window > Package Manager, set view to Unity Registry, install XR Interaction Toolkit and import starter assets, then install the Input System and confirm the editor restart. After restart, right-click Hierarchy and add XR > XR Origin (VR/Desktop) and delete the default Main Camera. Add a Plane named Ground at (0,0,0) scale (10,1,10). Add a Cube at (0,1,2), add a Rigidbody and uncheck Use Gravity, add XR Grab Interactable, and confirm the Collider is enabled. Connect your Meta Quest using Oculus Link or Air Link, then press Play. You should be able to look around and attempt a grab. If controllers do not respond, run the troubleshooting checklist: check Input Action Manager assignments and XR Controller action references. This activity is a complete path from a fresh project to a validated headset test.

keyIdea.title: Complete test path
keyIdea.text: This guided activity takes you from a fresh project to a working headset test using Oculus provider, toolkit, and a grabbable cube.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Meta Quest Setup & Test
Activity steps
  1. Create Unity 3D Core project.
  2. Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management → Android tab → enable Oculus and accept installs.
  3. Package Manager → install XR Interaction Toolkit and Input System; import starter assets and accept restart.
  4. Add XR Origin (VR/Desktop) and delete Main Camera.
  5. Add Ground plane and Cube with Rigidbody and XR Grab Interactable.
  6. Connect Meta Quest via Link and press Play to test grabbing.
Expected result

In Play mode with Link active you should see head tracking and be able to use the grip to pick up the cube if action assets are assigned correctly.

Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence exactly and validate wiring steps if controllers fail to respond.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Core terms and their short meanings

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts from this chapter so they are easy to recall. XR Plug-in Management is Unity's centralized mechanism for enabling the runtime providers your target headset requires. The XR Interaction Toolkit is a package that provides prefabs and components for common VR interactions like grabbing and teleporting; import its starter assets to get default input mappings and prefabs. The XR Origin is the player's in-scene representation that contains the camera offset, controllers, and the Input Action Manager which wires input actions to controller behaviors. Keep these terms in mind as you set up projects and diagnose issues. A quick habit: after installing packages, import the starter assets, assign the XRI Default Input Actions to the XR Origin's Input Action Manager, delete the default camera, and add a simple ground and a grabbable cube for immediate verification. This checklist captures the chapter's practical workflow and helps you move from installation to validated testing quickly.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Remember the plug-in provider, toolkit, XR Origin, and input actions are the pieces that must be installed and wired to get controllers and tracking working.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Key Concepts
XR Plug-in Management

Unity's system for enabling and installing VR/AR provider runtimes per platform.

XR Interaction Toolkit

A package with components and starter assets for common VR interactions such as grabbing.

XR Origin

A prefab representing the player's head and hands, containing the camera, controllers, and input manager.

Takeaway

Install the right provider, add the toolkit and Input System, assign action assets to XR Origin, and test with a ground and a grabbable cube.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three short reminders to guide setup and testing

narration.text: Here are three compact reminders to keep in mind while setting up your VR environment. First, always match the XR Plug-in provider to your target platform and accept Unity's package install prompts so the runtime is present. Second, install the XR Interaction Toolkit and the Input System, import starter assets, and assign the XRI Default Input Actions to the XR Origin's Input Action Manager so controller actions are available. Third, test early: add a ground plane and a grabbable cube with Rigidbody and collider, then use a Link connection to validate tracking and grabbing. These quick checks prevent many common errors and get you to productive iteration faster. As you move on, use this checklist whenever you create a new project so setup becomes routine rather than an obstacle.
